title: Filing an access-to-information request
content: Write to the information access officer describing the records sought, pay any prescribed fee, and keep proof of delivery. The body must respond within the statutory period. If refused, seek review by the Commission on Administrative Justice.

title: Constitution of Kenya, 2010 — Article 43
content: Article 43 recognises economic and social rights including accessible and adequate housing, reasonable standards of sanitation, health care, and social security. These rights are subject to progressive realisation and may only be limited as provided by law. Verify how a specific claim maps to this article with a legal aid provider.

title: Constitution of Kenya, 2010 — Article 47
content: Article 47 guarantees fair administrative action that is expeditious, efficient, lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair. A person affected by administrative action is entitled to written reasons. Keep copies of the decision, the notice received, and any written reasons given.

title: Constitution of Kenya, 2010 — Article 48
content: Article 48 requires the State to ensure access to justice for all persons. Where a person cannot afford legal representation and the interests of justice so require, representation may be provided at the State's expense. The National Legal Aid Service toll-free line is 0800 720 640.

title: Constitution of Kenya, 2010 — Article 50
content: Article 50 guarantees the right to a fair hearing, including having disputes resolved in a fair and public hearing before a court or tribunal. Accused persons have related rights including to be informed of the charge, to legal representation, and to bail where applicable. Verify procedure with a lawyer.

title: Rights and fundamental freedoms — scope
content: Article 19 explains that rights belong to individuals, preserve dignity, and bind the State and, where applicable, private persons. Limits must be justified under Article 24. When relying on a right, identify the specific article and how the facts fit it, then seek legal aid to test the claim.

title: Application of the Bill of Rights
content: Article 20 requires courts to interpret rights to favour their enforcement and to consider values like human dignity and equality. A person alleging a violation can go straight to the High Court. Keep a dated account of events, witnesses, and any documents showing the violation.

title: Implementation of rights and State duties
content: Article 21 obliges the State to observe, respect, protect, promote and fulfil rights, with progressive realisation for socio-economic rights within available resources. When petitioning an office, cite the duty and attach evidence of requests already made. Keep stamped copies of every petition.

title: Enforcing the Bill of Rights in court
content: Article 22 lets any person alleging a rights violation apply to the High Court for redress, and associations may act in the public interest. Formalities should be kept to a minimum. File a petition with an affidavit, the facts, the rights infringed, and the orders sought.

title: Relief the High Court may grant
content: Under Article 23 the High Court may declare rights violated, issue injunctions, order compensation, or grant conservatory orders to preserve the position pending hearing. Ask a lawyer which orders fit the urgency. Keep the petition, affidavits, and any interim orders together.

title: When rights may be limited
content: Article 24 permits limits only by law that is reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society, considering the nature and purpose of the limit. Some rights, such as freedom from torture, cannot be limited. Challenge any limit by asking the authority to cite the exact law.

title: Rights that cannot be limited
content: Article 25 protects freedom from torture and cruel treatment, slavery, and the right to a fair trial as non-limitable. Violations should be reported to police, IPOA where officers are involved, and a lawyer immediately. Preserve medical evidence and witness details.

title: Equality and freedom from discrimination
content: Article 27 guarantees equality before the law and bans discrimination on grounds including race, sex, pregnancy, disability, and religion. Affirmative action for marginalised groups is allowed. Record dates, comparators, and documents when lodging an equality complaint.

title: Human dignity protection
content: Article 28 declares every person has inherent dignity that must be respected and protected. Degrading treatment by officials or employers can ground complaints to oversight bodies and courts. Document what was said or done, where, and who witnessed it.

title: Freedom and security of the person
content: Article 29 protects against arbitrary detention, bodily harm, and psychological torture. Anyone detained must be told reasons and produced in court within 24 hours. Note the station, OB number, officers involved, and time of arrest for any follow-up.

title: Freedom from slavery and forced labour
content: Article 30 prohibits slavery, servitude, and forced labour. Workers held through threats, withheld documents, or debt bondage can report to police and the labour office and seek shelter support. Keep contracts, messages, and payment records as evidence.

title: Privacy as a constitutional right
content: Article 31 protects against search of person, home or property, seizure of possessions, and infringement of communications. Searches generally need lawful authority. Ask officers to identify the law and warrant, and note details without obstructing. Complain afterwards with a lawyer.

title: Freedom of conscience and religion
content: Article 32 protects freedom of conscience, religion, belief and opinion. No one may be compelled to act against belief except as law reasonably requires. Schools and employers should accommodate belief within reason. Put accommodation requests in writing.

title: Freedom of expression and its limits
content: Article 33 protects expression, media freedom, and academic freedom but excludes propaganda for war, incitement to violence, hate speech, and advocacy of hatred. Online posts can attract criminal complaints. Preserve links and timestamps and seek advice before responding publicly.

title: Freedom of the media
content: Article 34 guarantees media independence and bars State control over broadcasts or penalties for opinions. Complaints about media content go to the Media Complaints Commission. Keep broadcasts, articles, and dates when filing or answering a complaint.

title: Right of access to information
citation: Constitution of Kenya, 2010, Art. 35; Access to Information Act, 2016
content: Article 35 and the Access to Information Act let citizens request information held by the State and relevant private bodies. Requests go in writing to the information officer with a clear description. Keep the request copy, delivery proof, and the response deadline.

title: Assembly, demonstration and picketing
content: Article 37 protects peaceful assembly, demonstration and picketing. Organisers should notify police as required by the Public Order Act and keep events peaceful and unarmed. Carry the notification copy and organisers contacts during the event.

title: Political rights of citizens
content: Article 38 protects every citizen's right to form parties, contest elections, vote by secret ballot, and stand for office. Electoral disputes have strict timelines before the IEBC tribunal and election courts. Keep voter records, results forms, and objection receipts.

title: Freedom of movement and residence
content: Article 39 guarantees citizens freedom of movement, residence anywhere in Kenya, and the right to leave and return. Restrictions such as curfews must be lawful and published. Note the order relied upon and seek review if it seems unlawful.

title: Protection of the right to property
content: Article 40 protects the right to acquire and own property, with compulsory acquisition allowed only for public purpose with prompt full compensation. Do not surrender land without a written acquisition notice. Keep title deeds, valuations, and all notices.

title: Labour relations as a constitutional right
content: Article 41 guarantees fair labour practices, reasonable working conditions, the right to join unions, and the right to strike subject to law. Dismissals and union disputes can go to the Employment and Labour Relations Court. Keep contracts, payslips, and dispute correspondence.

title: Right to a clean and healthy environment
content: Article 42 guarantees a clean and healthy environment. Pollution, illegal dumping, and noisy operations can be reported to NEMA and county environment officers. Keep dated photos, a diary of incidents, and report reference numbers.

title: Economic and social rights claims
content: Article 43 covers health, housing, food, water, social security, and education. Claims proceed through petitions showing the State failure and the remedy sought. Attach prior complaints to the responsible office and their responses.

title: Language and cultural rights
content: Article 44 protects the right to use one's language and participate in cultural life. Cultural practices that violate rights, such as forced marriage, remain unlawful. Report harmful practices to chiefs, children officers, or police.

title: Family as the natural unit of society
content: Article 45 recognises the family as the fundamental unit of society and gives every adult the right to marry a person of the opposite sex with free consent. Parties to a marriage enjoy equal rights during and after marriage. Register marriages to protect property and children's rights.

title: Consumer rights in the Constitution
content: Article 46 gives consumers rights to goods of reasonable quality, information, health and safety, and compensation for loss from defective goods. This backs claims under the Consumer Protection Act. Keep receipts, warranties, and defect evidence.

title: Rights of arrested persons in detail
content: Article 49 requires an arrested person to be informed of reasons in an understandable language, allowed to contact counsel, and brought to court within 24 hours. Statements should not be forced. Memorise or note badge numbers, station, and OB entry.

title: Rights of detained and imprisoned persons
content: Article 51 preserves the dignity of detained persons including access to family, counsel, and medical care. Complaints about treatment go to the prison authorities, IPOA where relevant, and KNCHR. Keep visit records and medical notes.

title: Commission on Administrative Justice (Ombudsman)
citation: Constitution, Art. 59; Commission on Administrative Justice Act, 2011
content: The Ombudsman handles complaints about unfair, slow, or unresponsive public administration, such as delayed IDs, pensions, or land files. Complain first to the office, then to the Commission with reference numbers. Keep stamped copies and timelines.

title: National Gender and Equality Commission
content: The NGEC addresses gender, disability, youth, and minority discrimination in public and private institutions. Complaints should state the discriminatory act, dates, and witnesses. Keep policies, letters, and meeting notes as evidence.

title: Kenya National Commission on Human Rights
citation: Constitution of Kenya, 2010, Art. 59; KNCHR Act
content: The KNCHR investigates human rights violations, visits detention places, and can recommend redress. Complaints are lodged in writing with facts, dates, and evidence. Keep the complaint reference and follow-up correspondence.

title: Bill of Rights — general guidance
content: Chapter Four of the Constitution protects fundamental rights including equality, dignity, privacy, expression, and property. Rights may be limited only by law that is reasonable and justifiable. Enforcement is through the courts; keep a written record of what happened, when, and who was involved.

title: Delayed birth certificates
citation: Births and Deaths Registration Act, Cap. 149
content: Applications for birth certificates go through civil registration with hospital notification and parent IDs. Follow up in writing with the application number where delayed. Keep notification slips and payment receipts.

title: Complaining about a chief or assistant chief
content: Misconduct by a chief, such as demanding bribes for letters, can be reported to the Deputy County Commissioner with specifics. Keep copies of the request, any payment evidence, and witness names.

title: Petitioning a county assembly
content: Any person may petition a county assembly on matters within its authority, such as markets, health, or local roads. Petitions state facts, the relief sought, and attach evidence. Keep the filed copy with the clerk stamp.

title: County governments — general guidance
citation: Constitution of Kenya, 2010; County Governments Act, No. 17 of 2012
content: Many services such as business permits, markets, parking, and local rates are handled by county governments. Disputes about county fees or enforcement should start with the county office notice and receipts, then escalate through internal appeal or legal aid. Keep every receipt and notice.

title: County revenue and rate demands
citation: County Governments Act; county finance acts
content: County rate and fee demands state the property, period, and amount with payment points. Dispute errors in writing with receipts. Keep demand notes and payment records.

title: Devolution and which government to approach
citation: Constitution of Kenya, 2010, Ch. 11; County Governments Act, 2012
content: National government handles matters like immigration, tax, and courts while counties handle markets, local roads, health facilities, and business permits. Directing a complaint to the wrong level causes delay. Check the function list before filing and keep the referral letter.

title: Double allocation of market stalls
content: Where two traders hold papers for one stall, the county allocation register and fee receipts decide priority. Report to the market office with all documents and avoid taking the space by force. Keep allocation letters and payment records.

title: Checking voter registration details
content: Voters should verify registration status and polling station during the inspection period using IEBC channels. Report errors early with ID copies. Keep screenshots and correction receipts.

title: Demanding written reasons for admin action
citation: Constitution, Art. 47; Fair Administrative Action Act, 2015
content: A person affected by administrative action may demand written reasons. Make the demand in writing referencing the decision, date, and officer. The reasons reveal whether to appeal, seek review, or go to court.

title: Service complaints at Huduma Centres
content: Delays or demands for unofficial payment at service centres should be reported through the centre manager and the Huduma call line with the ticket number. Keep the service ticket, receipts, and names of officers seen.

title: Delayed national ID processing
content: First ID applications need a birth certificate, school documents, and chief introduction. Track the waiting slip and follow up at the registration office. Keep copies of all documents submitted.

title: Electoral complaints to IEBC
content: Election offences and registration problems can be reported to IEBC officials and monitors with polling station details and evidence. Formal election petitions go to the designated courts within strict timelines. Keep voter slips, results photos, and report numbers.

title: Judicial Service Commission complaints
content: Complaints about judicial officers go to the JSC in writing with the case number, dates, and conduct complained of. Matters pending in court should still be pursued through appeal or review. Keep filings and hearing records.

title: National Land Commission complaints
citation: Constitution, Art. 67; National Land Commission Act, 2012
content: The NLC investigates historical land injustices and monitors public land use. Complaints need the parcel details, history, and supporting documents. Keep title copies, maps, and correspondence with the lands office.

title: Land, environment and property rights — overview
content: The Constitution protects the right to property and sets principles for land policy including equitable access and security of land rights. Compulsory acquisition requires prompt and full compensation. Land disputes are commonly handled through the land registry, the Environment and Land Court, or alternative dispute resolution.

title: Public Service Commission recruitment disputes
content: Public service appointments must follow fair competition and merit. Candidates alleging bias can seek internal review with the advertisement, shortlist, and scores. Keep application receipts and interview invitations.

title: Nyumba Kumi community policing
citation: National Police Service community policing guidance
content: Nyumba Kumi clusters share security alerts with police and chiefs through cluster heads. Join the local cluster and save emergency contacts. Keep meeting notes.

title: Public finance complaints and county budgets
citation: Constitution, Ch. 12; Public Finance Management Act, 2012
content: Counties must publish budgets and allow public participation before spending. Residents can request budget documents and submit memoranda during participation forums. Keep adverts, submissions, and attendance records for any challenge.

title: Notifying police of a public meeting
content: Organisers of public meetings or processions should notify the police in writing in advance with the venue, route, date, and contacts. Carry the acknowledgement on the day. If restricted, ask for written reasons and consult a lawyer.

title: Public participation and petitions — general guidance
content: Public bodies must facilitate public participation, and every person has the right to petition public authorities. Put complaints and petitions in writing, keep a stamped copy, and note reference numbers and response dates for follow-up.

title: Salaries and Remuneration Commission queries
content: The SRC sets public officers pay and reviews allowances. Queries about public salary grading go through the employer and SRC advisories. Keep appointment letters, payslips, and grading correspondence.

title: Teachers Service Commission discipline
content: The TSC registers teachers and handles discipline and transfers. Teachers facing interdiction should respond in writing within the given time and attach evidence. Keep the show-cause letter, response, and hearing notices.

title: Using ward and sub-county offices
content: Ward administrators and sub-county officers handle local disputes, bursaries, and referrals with stamped records. Start there before headquarters. Keep referral slips.
